questions.question_text: Receptor responsible for malignant hyperthermia is?
questions.explanation: The source explanation describes malignant hyperthermia as a hypercatabolic state involving increased temperature, heart rate, carbon dioxide production, oxygen consumption, acidosis, muscle rigidity and rhabdomyolysis. It identifies a defect involving the ryanodine receptor.

questions.question_text: Agent causing malignant hyperthermia is?
questions.explanation: The source explains that malignant hyperthermia can be triggered by certain anesthetics and neuromuscular blocking agents. It describes uncontrolled calcium release from skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum and identifies dantrolene, cooling and supportive treatment.

questions.question_text: Pudendal nerve block involves?
questions.explanation: The source identifies the pudendal nerve roots as S2, S3 and S4. The nerve supplies the lower vagina, perineum and vulva.

questions.question_text: Drug used to reverse the effect of d-tubocurarine is:
Which of the following inhalational agents is the induction agent of choice in children?
questions.explanation: The source explains that sevoflurane is considered the inhalational induction agent of choice in children because it provides a pleasant, faster and smooth induction without significant systemic toxicity. Oxygen and nitrous oxide or halothane are also mentioned as alternatives.
references: Synopsis of Pediatric Emergency Medicine, 4th edition, page 34
Textbook of Anesthesia for Postgraduates, page 799

questions.question_text: Anesthetic agent with vasoconstrictor is contraindicated in?
questions.explanation: The source explains that vasoconstrictors such as epinephrine are usually avoided with local anesthetics in ring or finger blocks because severe vasoconstriction in end arteries can lead to gangrene.
references: Neural Blockade in Clinical Anesthesia and Management of Pain, page 124

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a sign of successful stellate ganglion block?
questions.explanation: The source states that bradycardia is not an established sign of a successful stellate ganglion block.
references: Short Textbook of Anesthesia, Ajay Yadav, 2nd edition, page 113
Atlas of Image-Guided Intervention in Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine, page 115

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old primigravida with a history of mitral stenosis and mitral regurgitation is in labour. She prefers a normal vaginal delivery. Which would be the best way to provide analgesia for this lady?
questions.explanation: The source explains that labour places significant stress on the cardiovascular system in patients with valvular heart disease. Epidural anaesthesia is preferred to reduce pain and sympathetic stimulation.

questions.question_text: Example of long acting neuromuscular blocker is:
questions.explanation: The source describes pancuronium as a long-acting neuromuscular blocker cleared largely by the kidney. It also discusses its hepatic uptake and metabolites.

questions.question_text: Tizanidine is a central alpha 2 adrenergic agonist. Assertion: It is indicated in painful muscle spasms of spinal origin. Reason: Because it inhibits the release of excitatory amino acids in spinal interneurons.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion
Assertion is true, but Reason is false
Assertion is false, but Reason is true

questions.explanation: Tizanidine is a central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. It inhibits the release of excitatory amino acids in spinal interneurons and facilitates the inhibitory transmitter glycine. It is indicated in painful muscle spasms of spinal origin.
references: Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, K.D. Tripathi, 5th edition, page 318

questions.question_text: Mechanism of action of theophylline in bronchial asthma include all of the following Except?
questions.explanation: The source lists phosphodiesterase inhibition, adenosine receptor antagonism and increased histone deacetylase activity among the proposed mechanisms of theophylline. Beta-2 receptor stimulation is not listed as its mechanism.

questions.question_text: Mendelson's syndrome is
questions.explanation: Mendelson's syndrome is due to aspiration of gastric contents. The source also mentions Sellick's manoeuvre as a preventive measure.

questions.question_text: Least blood gas partition coefficient anesthetic agent:
questions.explanation: The source identifies desflurane as the agent with the least blood-gas partition coefficient among the listed options.

questions.question_text: Stages of anesthesia were established by
questions.explanation: The source identifies ether as the agent associated with the establishment of the stages of anesthesia.

questions.question_text: Repeated use of halothane causes
questions.explanation: The source describes two types of halothane hepatotoxicity: a mild form with transient elevation of serum transaminases and a severe form characterized by centrilobular necrosis.

questions.question_text: Nephrotoxic agent is
questions.explanation: The source identifies methoxyflurane as the nephrotoxic agent among the listed options.

questions.question_text: Inhalational agent of choice in children:
questions.explanation: The source identifies sevoflurane as the inhalational agent of choice in children.

questions.question_text: In a 2 months old infant undergoing surgery for biliary atresia, you would avoid one of the following anaesthetic agents:
questions.explanation: The source identifies halothane as the agent to avoid because of its hepatotoxicity. It also notes that halothane hepatitis is associated with repeated exposure.

questions.question_text: A five-year old child is scheduled for strabismus (squint) correction. Induction of anesthesia is uneventful. After conjunctival incision as the surgeon grasps the medial rectus, the anaesthesiologist looks at the cardiac monitor. Why do you think he did that?

options.text: He wanted to check the depth of anaesthesia
He wanted to be sure that the blood pressure did not fall
He wanted to see if there was an oculocardiac reflex
He wanted to make sure there were no ventricular dysrhythmias which normally accompany incision

questions.explanation: Traction on extraocular muscles or pressure on the eyeball can elicit cardiac dysrhythmias ranging from bradycardia to sinus arrest. This reflex has a trigeminal afferent and vagal efferent pathway and is common in children undergoing strabismus surgery.

questions.question_text: Treatment of malignant hyperthermia includes:
questions.explanation: Dantrolene and active cooling are important measures in the treatment of malignant hyperthermia.

questions.question_text: Which statements are true about adrenaline in CPR?

options.text: IV route is better than intracardiac
Intracardiac route is better than IV

questions.explanation: The source identifies intratracheal administration as possible and the IV route as preferable to the intracardiac route.

questions.question_text: From which route is absorption of local anaesthetic maximum?
questions.explanation: Systemic absorption is related to blood supply. Intercostal administration produces high systemic absorption.

questions.question_text: Which description defines allodynia during pain management?

options.text: Unpleasant sensation with or without a stimulus
Perception of an ordinarily non-noxious stimulus as severe pain

questions.explanation: Allodynia is pain caused by a stimulus that would not normally produce pain.

questions.question_text: Which drug produces dissociative anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: Ketamine produces dissociative anaesthesia and profound analgesia.

questions.question_text: Which anaesthetic agent also has anti-emetic property?
questions.explanation: Propofol has anti-emetic properties.

questions.question_text: Which statement about halothane is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Halothane causes bronchodilation rather than bronchoconstriction.

questions.question_text: Which is the longest-acting muscle relaxant among the following?
questions.explanation: Among the listed options, doxacurium is identified as the longest-acting agent in the source.

questions.question_text: Which is the shortest-acting non-depolarizing muscle relaxant?
questions.explanation: Mivacurium is the shortest-acting non-depolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant.

questions.question_text: What is the standard method to differentiate between endotracheal and oesophageal intubation?
questions.explanation: Detection of exhaled carbon dioxide using capnography is the standard confirmation method.

questions.question_text: The action of which anaesthetic agent is through NMDA receptors?
questions.explanation: Xenon exerts anaesthetic action partly through non-competitive blockade of NMDA receptors.

questions.question_text: Which is the most sensitive method of non-invasive monitoring of cardiovascular ischaemia in the perioperative period?
questions.explanation: Two-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography can detect regional wall-motion abnormalities and myocardial ischaemia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT an amide local anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Procaine is an ester local anaesthetic.

questions.question_text: Which is the shortest-acting skeletal muscle relaxant?
questions.explanation: Suxamethonium (succinylcholine) is the shortest-acting skeletal muscle relaxant.

questions.question_text: In epidural anaesthesia, where is the drug injected?
questions.explanation: Epidural medication is administered into the epidural space, outside the dura mater.

questions.question_text: All of the following are true about coeliac plexus block EXCEPT:

options.text: Can provide anaesthesia for intra-abdominal surgery
Can be given only by the retrocrural approach

questions.explanation: Approaches include retrocrural, anterocrural and splanchnic nerve block techniques.

questions.question_text: Mild systemic disease is included in which ASA grade?
questions.explanation: ASA II describes a patient with mild systemic disease.

questions.question_text: All are contraindications of spinal anaesthesia EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hypertension alone is not listed as an absolute contraindication in this question.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT an intravenous anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Cyclopropane is an inhalational anaesthetic agent.

questions.question_text: What is the index of potency of general anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: MAC is used as a measure of the potency of inhalational anaesthetic agents.

questions.question_text: Which modification of the Mapleson E breathing system is used in infants?
questions.explanation: Mapleson F is the Jackson-Rees modification of Mapleson E and is used in neonates, infants and small children.

questions.question_text: Which inhalational agent is preferred in head injury with raised intracranial tension?
questions.explanation: The source identifies isoflurane as causing a relatively small increase in intracranial tension.

questions.question_text: Malignant hyperthermia is caused by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia involves uncontrolled release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.question_text: Which muscle relaxant causes maximum histamine release?
questions.explanation: The source explanation identifies d-tubocurarine as having the greatest tendency to release histamine.

questions.question_text: A patient on atracurium develops seizures due to accumulation of which substance?
questions.explanation: Laudanosine is a metabolite of atracurium.

questions.question_text: The ideal parameters for cardiac massage in CPR are all EXCEPT:

options.text: Force should depress sternum by 1.5 inches
Ratio of compression to ventilation should be 15:2
Compressions should be given over the lower third of sternum
Force should depress sternum approximately one-third of chest wall diameter

questions.explanation: The source marks the 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio as the exception.

questions.question_text: Probable indicators of reversal of neuromuscular blockade are all EXCEPT:

options.text: Ability to perform sustained tongue depressor test

questions.explanation: The source lists a 5-second leg lift, not a 10-second leg lift, among the clinical indicators.

questions.question_text: In spinal anaesthesia, the drug is deposited between which structures?
questions.explanation: Spinal anaesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space between the pia and arachnoid mater.

questions.question_text: Diffusion hypoxia is seen during which period?
questions.explanation: During recovery, nitrous oxide diffuses from blood into the alveoli and dilutes alveolar oxygen.

questions.question_text: Which muscle relaxant can be used as an alternative to succinylcholine during endotracheal intubation?
questions.explanation: The source identifies mivacurium as the alternative among the listed options.

questions.question_text: Which ventilation mode is NOT used for weaning?
questions.explanation: Controlled mechanical ventilation does not provide the spontaneous breathing support used in common weaning strategies.

questions.question_text: About lignocaine, all are true EXCEPT:

options.text: It belongs to the ester group of local anaesthetics
It can penetrate through mucous membrane

questions.explanation: Lignocaine is an amide local anaesthetic, not an ester.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT commonly used as an induction agent?
questions.explanation: The source identifies midazolam as the option not commonly used as an induction agent in this question.

questions.question_text: All of the following anaesthetics are used in children EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The source identifies desflurane as the exception, particularly because of airway irritation during inhalational induction.

questions.question_text: Which gas cylinder has a single pin index?
questions.explanation: The source identifies Entonox as the answer.

questions.question_text: Halothane causes:
questions.explanation: The source lists bradycardia, reduced blood pressure and uterine relaxation as effects of halothane.

questions.question_text: Speed of onset of action of inhalational anaesthetics is indicated by:
questions.explanation: The blood-gas partition coefficient reflects blood solubility and influences induction and recovery speed.

questions.question_text: What is a use of dexmedetomidine?

options.text: Prolongs action of local anaesthetic in hypertensive patients
Increases bioavailability of regional anaesthetic drug
Helps reduce BIS of a general anaesthetic drug with low potency

questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist used for sedation in intubated patients.

questions.question_text: Which local anaesthetic is used in wound or ulcer management for topical anaesthetic action?
questions.explanation: Benzocaine has topical anaesthetic action.

questions.question_text: Which is the most commonly used local anaesthetic among the following options?
questions.explanation: The source identifies bupivacaine as the answer among the listed options; lignocaine is more commonly used overall.

questions.question_text: What is the second gas effect?

options.text: Displacement of nitrous oxide by oxygen
Displacement of oxygen by nitrous oxide
Facilitation of inhalation of halothane by nitrous oxide
Removal of oxygen by nitrous oxide from alveoli during recovery

questions.explanation: Rapid uptake of nitrous oxide can concentrate other inhaled gases in the alveoli and facilitate their uptake.

questions.question_text: Dibucaine number refers to:
questions.explanation: Dibucaine number is used to assess atypical pseudocholinesterase activity.

questions.question_text: Which local anaesthetic has the maximum ionized form at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: The source identifies chloroprocaine as the answer.

questions.question_text: All of the following are advantages of LMA EXCEPT:

options.text: Does not require laryngoscope and visualization

questions.explanation: A standard LMA does not reliably protect against aspiration.

questions.question_text: Which stage of anaesthesia is the stage of analgesia?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 is the stage of analgesia in the classical stages of general anaesthesia.

questions.question_text: Ketamine acts on which receptor?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist.

questions.question_text: Succinylcholine causes hyperkalaemia in patients with:
questions.explanation: The source identifies burns, severe infection and high-velocity trauma as risk settings.

questions.question_text: Which is a long-acting local anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Dibucaine is a long-acting local anaesthetic.

questions.question_text: Modern monitors used to measure ETCO2 make use of:
questions.explanation: Modern capnography monitors commonly use infrared absorption spectroscopy.

questions.question_text: Which machine is used non-invasively to monitor external chest compressions during CPR?

options.text: Zoll AED Plus automatic external defibrillator

questions.explanation: The Zoll AED Plus compression pad includes an accelerometer to monitor compression depth.

questions.question_text: What is the most important factor determining the effect of an anaesthetic agent on the fetus?
questions.explanation: The source identifies the duration of pregnancy as the most important factor.

questions.question_text: Regarding propofol, which of the following is false?

options.text: It is used as an intravenous induction agent
It is painful on intravenous injection
It has no muscle relaxant property

questions.explanation: Propofol has anti-emetic properties rather than causing severe vomiting.

questions.question_text: Eutectic mixture of local anaesthetic (EMLA) cream contains:
questions.explanation: EMLA is a topical mixture of 2.5% lidocaine and 2.5% prilocaine.

questions.question_text: Which skeletal muscle relaxant undergoes Hoffmann elimination?
questions.explanation: Atracurium undergoes Hoffmann elimination and ester hydrolysis.

questions.question_text: Which is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Bupivacaine is associated with significant cardiotoxicity.

questions.question_text: What concentration of adrenaline is used with lignocaine for local infiltration in this question?
questions.explanation: The source answer is 1:50,000.

questions.question_text: Local anaesthetics act by:

options.text: Sodium channel inhibition from the inside
Sodium channel inhibition from the outside
Potassium channel inhibition from the inside
Potassium channel inhibition from the outside

questions.explanation: Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels from the intracellular side.

questions.question_text: Thiopentone is contraindicated in:
questions.explanation: Thiopentone is contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria because it can precipitate an acute attack.

questions.question_text: Pre-anaesthetic medication is given for:
questions.explanation: Premedication can reduce anxiety, secretions and undesirable reflexes, among other purposes.

questions.question_text: All are true about post-spinal headache EXCEPT:

options.text: Can be prevented by using a small-bore needle
Old age is a risk factor

questions.explanation: Young age, rather than old age, is a recognised risk factor for post-dural puncture headache.

questions.question_text: IV administration of which anaesthetic drug is most painful?
questions.explanation: Propofol is commonly associated with pain on intravenous injection.

questions.question_text: Which is the most common method used to assess depth of anaesthesia in this question?
questions.explanation: Bispectral index uses processed EEG data to estimate depth of anaesthesia.

questions.question_text: During laryngoscopy and intubation, all of the following are true EXCEPT:

options.text: Slight pressure may be applied at the cricoid cartilage
The laryngoscope is held in the right hand
The neck is flexed with extension at the atlanto-occipital joint
The laryngoscope is levered on the upper incisor to lift the tongue

questions.explanation: The laryngoscope should not be hinged against the teeth.

questions.question_text: Drug of choice for reversal of neuromuscular blockade by vecuronium:
questions.explanation: Sugammadex binds aminosteroid neuromuscular blockers including vecuronium and rocuronium.

questions.question_text: Current recommendation for minimum preoperative fasting period for solid food (light meal):
questions.explanation: The source gives 6 hours for a light meal. Fasting recommendations differ for heavier meals.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists update report

questions.question_text: A patient under general anaesthesia suddenly develops tachycardia, sweating, hypertension and tachypnoea. What is the best immediate step?
questions.explanation: These findings may indicate inadequate depth of anaesthesia. The source recommends deepening anaesthesia immediately.

questions.question_text: What are the reasons for difficult intubation in an obese patient?
questions.explanation: Obesity can make airway visualisation difficult and reduce functional residual capacity and safe apnoea time.

questions.question_text: Positive end-expiratory pressure causes an increase in which respiratory parameters according to the source?
questions.explanation: PEEP can recruit alveoli and increase functional residual capacity. Its effects on compliance and tidal volume depend on the clinical setting.

questions.question_text: Capnography is used for which of the following according to the source?

options.text: Amount of CO2 transported in blood

questions.explanation: A sudden or unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 can be an important sign of malignant hyperthermia.

questions.question_text: What is NOT true about preoperative modification of drugs?

options.text: Lithium should be stopped 2–3 days before
Low-dose aspirin should be stopped 7 days before
Tricyclic antidepressants can be continued until the date of operation
Oral anticoagulants are stopped 4 days before

questions.explanation: The source states that low-dose aspirin may be continued until the day of surgery; perioperative decisions should be individualised.

questions.question_text: ASA grading in anaesthesia is used to assess:
questions.explanation: The ASA Physical Status Classification describes a patient's pre-anaesthesia physical status.

questions.question_text: A brain-dead patient comes under which category in ASA classification?
questions.explanation: ASA VI describes a declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following prevents aspiration?
questions.explanation: The ProSeal LMA includes a gastric drainage tube. It offers improved separation of the respiratory and gastrointestinal pathways, but it does not provide the same protection as a cuffed tracheal tube.

questions.question_text: When shifting a patient from assisted ventilation to voluntary ventilation, which finding indicates failure?
questions.explanation: Severe oxygen desaturation indicates failure of a spontaneous breathing or weaning attempt.

questions.question_text: Tracheostomy reduces dead space by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Tracheostomy bypasses the upper airway and reduces anatomical dead space.

questions.question_text: VAT in mechanical ventilation stands for:
questions.explanation: VAT stands for ventilator-associated tracheobronchitis.

questions.question_text: What is the best anaesthesia for low forceps delivery?
questions.explanation: A saddle block can provide anaesthesia for outlet or low forceps delivery.

questions.question_text: What is the site of topical block of the sphenopalatine ganglion?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine foramen is near the posterior end of the middle turbinate.
references: Morgan, 4th edition, Chapter 78; Lee's Synopsis of Anaesthesia, 13th edition, page 411; Dhingra, 4th edition, page 131

questions.question_text: What is the sequence of CPR?
questions.explanation: The source gives the sequence as basic life support, defibrillation and advanced cardiac life support.
references: 2010 International Consensus on Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care Science

questions.question_text: Endotracheal tube cuff pressure during prolonged ventilation should be less than:
questions.explanation: The source answer is below 20 mm Hg. Cuff pressure is commonly monitored to reduce tracheal mucosal injury.

questions.question_text: What percentage of halothane is metabolised?
questions.explanation: Approximately 20% of halothane undergoes hepatic metabolism according to the source.

questions.question_text: A heavy smoker scheduled for elective hernia repair should stop smoking how long before surgery?
questions.explanation: The source recommends 6–8 weeks of smoking cessation before surgery to reduce pulmonary complications.

questions.question_text: Which was the first drug used as a local anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Cocaine was first used as a local anaesthetic by Carl Koller for corneal anaesthesia.

questions.question_text: Maintenance of anaesthesia in a 70-year-old male for surgery lasting 4–6 hours should ideally include which combination?
questions.explanation: The source identifies the combination of oxygen, air, desflurane, atracurium and remifentanil.
references: Miller's Anesthesiology, 7th edition, Chapters 7 and 28; Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease

questions.question_text: Which tidal volume setting should be used in a patient with ARDS according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source answer is 5–7 ml/kg. Contemporary lung-protective ventilation commonly targets approximately 6 ml/kg of predicted body weight.
references: Miller's Anesthesiology, 7th edition, Chapter 91; Journal of Thoracic Disease, 2013, Issue 5(3), page 323–334

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is used in CPR?
questions.explanation: Amiodarone is used in cardiac arrest algorithms for selected shock-refractory ventricular arrhythmias.
references: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC, 2010

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension, on ACE inhibitors and antiplatelet medication, with a history of CABG 4 years ago, is scheduled for hernia surgery. He has good effort tolerance. Which of the following preoperative investigations are ordered?

options.text: Routine preoperative evaluation and clinical evaluation
Routine preoperative evaluation, clinical evaluation and stress testing
Routine preoperative evaluation, clinical evaluation and angiography to look for patency
Routine preoperative evaluation, clinical evaluation and V/Q scan

questions.explanation: The source marks option A. The patient is described as having good effort tolerance. The source does not provide a detailed explanation.

questions.question_text: Cisatracurium is preferred over atracurium due to which advantage?
questions.explanation: According to the source, cisatracurium does not produce the consistent dose-dependent histamine release associated with atracurium.

questions.question_text: Laudanosine is a metabolite of which drug?
questions.explanation: The source identifies atracurium as the answer. It also explains that both atracurium and cisatracurium undergo Hofmann elimination and produce laudanosine.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a controlled-delivery device used to deliver a fixed concentration of oxygen?
questions.explanation: A Venturi mask delivers a controlled oxygen concentration by entraining a predictable amount of room air.

questions.question_text: All of the following are components of the WHO 19-point Surgical Safety Checklist, EXCEPT:

options.text: Mark the correct site for surgery
Give an antibiotic within 60 minutes of making an incision

questions.explanation: The source identifies all three listed measures as checklist components, making 'None of the above' the answer.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum dose of lignocaine that can be given with adrenaline for ocular blocks, according to the source?
questions.explanation: The PDF states a maximum lignocaine dose of 7 mg/kg when combined with adrenaline.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can lower EEG amplitude?
questions.explanation: The source identifies hypothermia as a cause of EEG depression and reduced amplitude.

questions.question_text: Which statement is NOT true about xenon anesthesia?

options.text: It has minimal cardiovascular side effects
It has slow induction and slow recovery
It inhibits the calcium pump and has low blood-gas solubility

questions.explanation: The source marks slow induction and slow recovery as the incorrect statement about xenon anesthesia.

questions.question_text: At the end of anesthesia, after discontinuation of nitrous oxide and removal of the endotracheal tube, 100% oxygen is administered to prevent:
questions.explanation: After nitrous oxide is discontinued, it diffuses from blood into the alveoli and dilutes alveolar oxygen. This can cause diffusion hypoxia.

questions.question_text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with head injury, BP 90/60 mmHg and pulse 150/min. Which anesthetic agent should be used for induction, according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source gives thiopentone as the answer for induction in this head-injury question.

questions.question_text: Which afferent nerve fibre is affected first by local anesthesia?
questions.explanation: The PDF identifies Type C fibres as the answer.

questions.question_text: Central neuraxial (spinal and epidural) anesthesia is NOT contraindicated in which of the following?
questions.explanation: The source identifies aspirin use as the answer and notes that aspirin and NSAIDs are generally not associated with increased neuraxial bleeding risk in the way anticoagulants can be. Clinical decisions require individual assessment.

questions.question_text: All of the following are induction agents EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The source identifies nitrous oxide as the exception. The question is labelled September 2007 in the PDF.

questions.question_text: EEG monitoring in anesthesia is useful for assessing:
questions.explanation: EEG-based monitoring can help assess the depth of general anesthesia. The source also discusses BIS monitoring.

questions.question_text: A patient with hypertension controlled by medication falls under which ASA physical status grade, according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source classifies a patient with controlled hypertension and mild systemic disease without functional limitation as ASA II.

questions.question_text: Modified Allen's test is used to check proper arterial supply at the:
questions.explanation: The PDF identifies the wrist as the answer for the Modified Allen's test.

questions.question_text: Which is the most potent analgesic agent among the following?
questions.explanation: The source identifies nitrous oxide as the most potent analgesic among the listed options.

questions.question_text: The dose of which muscle relaxant should be calculated using total body weight rather than ideal body weight in an obese person, according to the source?
questions.explanation: The PDF gives atracurium as the answer. Verify this dosing recommendation against current clinical references before using it as a clinical guide.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child is intubated for craniotomy. The anesthesia machine suddenly starts showing bellows movement. What is the next management?
questions.explanation: The source marks a larger endotracheal tube as the answer, but explicitly states that the recalled question is incomplete. The original clinical context is unclear.

questions.question_text: An infant with respiratory distress is intubated. What is the fastest and most accurate method to confirm intubation?
questions.explanation: The source identifies capnography as the fastest and accurate method for confirming tracheal intubation.

questions.question_text: Which statement about lidocaine is false?

options.text: It is an amide local anesthetic
It is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic
It can be used for local anesthesia
It is available in injectable preparations

questions.explanation: The source identifies the claim that lidocaine is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic as false.

questions.question_text: In a pregnant female, spinal anesthetic requirement is decreased due to all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Increased sensitivity of nerves to anesthetic agents

questions.explanation: The source identifies exaggerated lumbar lordosis as the exception. Decreased CSF volume, epidural venous engorgement and increased nerve sensitivity contribute to reduced spinal anesthetic requirements.

questions.question_text: After eye surgery under propofol and succinylcholine anesthesia, a patient develops leg pain while walking 8 hours later. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine can cause initial muscle fasciculations followed by postoperative muscle soreness.

questions.question_text: A spontaneously breathing 20-year-old patient undergoes incision and drainage under general anesthesia. Which breathing circuit is preferred for spontaneous ventilation?
questions.explanation: Mapleson A, also called the Magill circuit, is the circuit of choice for spontaneous ventilation according to the source.

questions.question_text: Which of the following agents is used in day-care surgery?
questions.explanation: Propofol is widely used as an induction agent in day-care anesthesia because of rapid recovery and a low incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting.

questions.question_text: All of the following are methods for improving oxygenation using a ventilator, EXCEPT:

options.text: Low tidal volume with high PEEP

questions.explanation: The source identifies high-frequency ventilation as the exception in this question.

questions.question_text: The names Brechner and Bethune are associated with which device?
questions.explanation: The source associates Brechner and Bethune with end-tidal capnography.

questions.question_text: A patient with head injury is intubated and ventilated. What is the ideal mode of ventilation according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source identifies controlled mechanical ventilation (CMV) as the answer.

questions.question_text: What is the appropriate LMA size for an average adult patient weighing 50 kg?
questions.explanation: The source gives LMA size 4.0 for an average adult weighing 50 kg.

questions.question_text: The plane of surgical anesthesia during ether anesthesia is defined as:

options.text: Loss of consciousness to onset of spontaneous respiration
From onset of regular respiration to cessation of spontaneous breathing

questions.explanation: Stage III, the stage of surgical anesthesia, extends from the beginning of regular respiration to cessation of spontaneous breathing.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs does NOT affect absorption and secretion of cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation: The source identifies nitrous oxide as the answer.

questions.question_text: Which intravenous anesthetic agent is contraindicated in epileptic patients posted for general anesthesia, according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source identifies ketamine as the answer.

questions.question_text: Midazolam causes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Decreased cardiovascular effects compared with propofol

questions.explanation: The source identifies retrograde amnesia as the exception. Midazolam is associated with anterograde amnesia.

questions.question_text: What is the shelf life of suxamethonium according to the source?

adrenal glands.

nervous system, this block may help to reduce stress and endocrine

complication of celiac plexus block is postural hypotenstion because
of blockade of lumbar sympathetic chain leading to upper abdominal
vessel dilation and venous pooling.

splanchnic nerve block.

pancreatitis, gastric & pancreatic malignancies.

Brachial plexus block
This is the second most commonly practised block after central
neuraxial block (spinal & epidural anaesthesia). Brachial plexus
block is used for upper limb surgeries.
Brachial plexus can be blocked by 4 approaches : -
1. Interscalene approach
Brachial plexus is blocked between anterior and middle scalene.
This approach is not used routinely due to close proximity of vital
structures. Ulnar nerve is usually spared by this approach because
injection is given in close proximity of upper nerve roots and inferior
nerve roots (C8-T 1) may be spared.
This technique provides excellent anaesthesia and analgesia for
shoulder and upper arm procedures. (in contrast to other three
approaches which do not provide adequate shoulder anaesthesia).
Complications include Horner syndrome (due to stellate ganglion
block), phrenic nerve block, intravascular injection into carotids and
epidural or intrathecal injections.
2. Supraclavicular approach
This is the most commonly used approach. It involves the injection
of local anaesthetic in close proximity to

the trunks of the brachial plexus by inserting the needle lateral to
subclavian vessels. The supraclavicular
block is performed where the brachial plexus is most compact,
consequently, it produces reliable and rapid
onset anaesthesia and is particularly useful in a fast paced
ambulatory surgery centre.
Pneumothorax is the most common complication. Other
complications include phrenic nerve block, intravascular injection in
subclavian artery or vein, Horner syndrome, hematoma formation.
3. Infra-clavicular approach
 Infraclavicular block involves the injection of local anaesthetic in
close proximity of cords of the brachial plexus. The axillary nerve
may be spared as this nerve exits the brachial plexus sheath
proximal to the level of infraclavicular block.
4. Axillary approach
Axillary block involves the injection of local anaesthetic in close
proximity of terminal branches of the
brachial plexus. The major disadvantage of this approach is that
mucocutaneous and intercostobrachial nerves are spared. So arm
surgery cannot be performed. In contrast to interscalene approach,
most intense
block occur in (C7-T1) ulnar dermatomes and least in C5-C6
dermatomes.

Intravenous regional Anaesthesia (Bier's block)
Intravenous regional anaesthesia (IVRA) is used most often for
surgery of the forearm and hand, but can also be used for distal leg
and foot.

Then tourniquet cuff is applied to proximal arm.

→ocal anaesthetic can not be drained out from upper limb and can
not enter in systemic circulation because of inflated cuff in proximal
arm.
The arm is anaesthetized in 6-8 minutes.

technique.               —Goodman & Gilman llthie 381 o A few
clinician prefers prilocaine over lidocaine because of its higher
therapeutic index - least toxic LA.

etidocaine are contraindicated for Bier's block.

questions.question_text: Longest part of optic nerve ?
questions.explanation:

Optic nerve
Each optic nerve (second cranial nerve) starts from the optic disc
and extends up to optic chiasma, where the two nerves meet.
It is the backward continuation of the nerve fibre layer of the retina,
which consists of the second order neurons i.e., axon originating
from the ganglion cells.
It also contains the afferent fibres of the papillary light reflex.
Morphologically and embryologically, the optic nerve is comparable
to a sensory tract.
Unlike peripheral nerves it is not covered by neurilemma (so it does
not regenerate when cut).
The fibres of optic nerve, numbering about a million, are very fine (2-
10 m in diameter as compared to 20 mm of sensory nerves).
Optic nerve is about 47-50 mm in length and can be divided into 4
parts : ?
Intraocular part (1 mm) : - It begins at optic disc (optic nerve head)
and exits the nerve through a hole in sclera that is occupied by a
mesh like structure called the lamina cribrosa. The nerve fibres from
the retina leave the eye through pores (holes) in lamina cribrosa, a
sieve-like structure made up of collagen meshwork.
Intraorbital part (30 mm) : - Extends from back of the eyeball (at

lamina cribrosa) to the optic foramina.
Intracanalicular part (6-9 mm) : - It lies within the optic canal and
closely related to ophthalmic artery which crosses obliquely over it.
Intracranial part (10 mm) : - It lies above the cavernous sinus and
converges with its fellow from contralateral side to form optic
chiasma.
Like other parts of CNS, the optic nerve is covered by meningeal
sheaths (Pia, archnoid and dura mater) as soon as the nerve leaves
the eyeball.

Photoretinitis refers to damage to the retina resulting from exposure

of the retina to shorter wave-length in the visible spectrum (i.e.

observing, telescopy solar viewing, watching bright sunlight, or
exposure to the flash of the short-circuiting of a strong current.

into positive scotoma, and metamorphosia.

seen at the fovea with a brownish-red ring around it.

around the fovea, or even the formation of retinal hole

Ptosis is drooping of upper eyelid. Ptosis occurs when the muscles
that raise the eyelid (levator palpebrae superiors and muller's
nuscles) are not strong enough to do so properly. Etiology of Ptosis
may be :?

ptosis and is often bilateral.
It is associated with maldevelopment or congenital weakness of
levator palpebrae sperioris. Congenital myogenic ptosis is
characterized by drooping of one or both lids at birth, with a
diminished or absent lid crease and lid lag on downgaze due to
tethering effect of abnormal muscle. It may occur in following forms
Simple congenital ptosis :- Not associated with other anomaly
Congenital ptosis with superior rectus weakness
Blepharophimosis syndrome Congenital ptosis, blepharophimosis,
telecanthus and epicanthus inversus.
Congenital synkinetic ptosis (Marcus Gunn jaw- winking Ptosis):-
Retraction of ptotic lid with jaw movement like chewing, i.e., with
stimulation of ipsilateral pterygoid muscle.
B) Acquird ptosis :- Depending upon the cause acquired ptosis
may be

Neurogenic :- It is due to paralysis of 3rd nerve, Horner's syndrome,
ophthalmoplegic migraine, multiple sclerosis. Neurogenic ptosis may
also occur due to lesion of sympathetic nerve) supplying muller's
muscle.
 Myogenic :- It is due to acquired defect of LPS muscle and may be
seen in myasthenia gravis, dystrophia myotonica, ocular myopathy,
oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, thyrotoxicosis, Lambert -
Eaton mysthenia syndrome

scarring (cicatracial ptosis) in atients with ocular pemphigoid and
trachoma.

Histology of cornea
The cornea has five distinct layers (from superficial to deep) : ?
Epithelium : - It is the outermost part of cornea and is composed of
stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelial cells.
Bowman's membrane : - It is not a true membrane but simply a
condensed superficial part of stroma. destroyed, it does not
regenerate.
Stroma (Substantia propria) : - This layer constitutes most of the
cornea (90% of thickness). It consists of collagen fibrils (lamellae)
embedded in hydrated matrix ofproteoglycans.
Descemet's membrane : - This layer bounds the stroma posteriorly.
In the periphery it appears to end at the anterior limit of trabecular
meshwork as Schwahle's ring.
Endothelium : - It is a single layer of flat polygnonal cells. The
endothelial cells contain 'active-pump' mechanism and is the most
important layer in maintaining the transparency of cornea.

questions.question_text: Most effective circuit in spontaneous anaesthesia is -

Answer: A - Mapleson A
MAPLESON A - (Magill) CIRCUIT
Useful in spontaneous ventilation
The patient inspires whatever is in the tube, using the bag as a
volume reservoir.
On eated tube and incoming fresh gas. When the bag is full, exhaled
alveolar gas is vented frxpiration, the bag refills from a combination
of expired gas going back up the corrugom the exhale valve, and
then during any expiratory pause, FGF pushes the remaining
alveolar gas out.
Theoretically FGF = 0.7 x Valv should prevent significant rebreathing
because deadspace gas (fresh) is not wasted, but FGF = VA more
reliably prevents rebreathing.
Tube volume must exceed (Vt-Vd) or alveolar gas could contaminate
the bag.
Inadequate FGF causes rebreathing . Difficult to detect from the
CO2 waveform alone - all that happens is that the rapid fall on
inspiration is delayed. If VA exceeds tubing volume, CO2 enters the
bag and will be seen on inspiration on the capnogram.
Controlled ventilation
If the anaesthetist fully closed the valve while squeezing the bag and

didn't open it until just before the bag filled, this circuit would be OK.
More commonly the valve is partially closed - enough to permit
adequate tidal volumes despite parallel loss of gas out the valve.
FGF must be increased to compensate for gas lost during inspiration
- typically 2.5x minute ventilation.
The Lack system
A co-axial Magill, with the expiratory valve brought coaxially back to
the Fresh Gas outlet. Not popular due to inefficiency during
controlled ventilation.
